fields.title: Data Integration and Transformation Using Power Query - Proficient
fields.instructions: Use the uploaded Basic assignment document as the authoritative task and rubric source.
tasks: Connect to the provided Sales, Product, and Store data files.
Profile the datasets and identify data quality issues.
Remove duplicate transaction records.
Handle blank and null values appropriately.
Correct incorrect data types.
Standardize inconsistent date formats.
Standardize inconsistent naming conventions.
Rename columns using meaningful and consistent names.
Split or merge columns where appropriate.
Remove unnecessary columns.
Apply appropriate basic Power Query transformations.
Load the transformed datasets into Power BI.
deliverables: Short data preparation report covering data quality issues, transformations, and rationale
fields.expected_outcome: A clean, consistent, and analysis-ready dataset that can be used for data modelling and reporting.

fields.title: DAX Measures and Analytical Calculations - Foundation
fields.instructions: Use the uploaded Basic assignment document as the authoritative task and rubric source.
tasks: Create 3-5 DAX measures such as Total Sales, Total Quantity Sold, Average Sales, Number of Transactions, and Total Profit.
Create at least one calculated column such as Profit = Sales Amount - Cost Amount.
Use basic DAX functions including SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, and DISTINCTCOUNT.
Validate calculations against source data.
Explain the business meaning of the metrics.
deliverables: Short explanation of how metrics support decision-making
fields.expected_outcome: A set of accurate DAX measures and calculated columns that provide meaningful business metrics for analysing sales performance.

fields.title: Analytical Data Modelling, Relationships and Hierarchies - Proficient
fields.instructions: Use the uploaded Basic assignment document as the authoritative task and rubric source.
tasks: Create a Sales fact table.
Create Product, Store, and Date dimension tables.
Establish relationships between the fact and dimension tables.
Configure appropriate one-to-many cardinality.
Create a Product hierarchy with Category and Product.
Create a Date hierarchy with Year, Quarter, Month, and Date.
Organize the model clearly and logically.
Validate the model using sample data analysis.
fields.expected_outcome: A functional basic star-schema data model that enables accurate analysis of sales across products, stores, regions, and time.

fields.title: Informative Reports and Interactive Executive Dashboard - Foundation

Strong closing line
The goal is not only to know data science. The goal is to demonstrate that you can apply it.
Q4. What is the difference between learners who successfully
switch careers and those who do not?
Main answer
The biggest difference is usually not talent. It is ownership.
Successful career switchers normally do five things.
First, they are consistent. They practise even when the topic is difficult.
Second, they ask questions early. They do not remain silent for several weeks and only reveal at the end that
they are lost.
Third, they build a portfolio. They understand that completing a course is only one part of the journey.
Employers need evidence of what they can do.
Fourth, they connect their previous experience to data. Someone from logistics can analyse delivery
performance. Someone from finance can work on risk or transaction data. Someone from retail can study
customer behaviour.
Finally, they are flexible about their first role. They do not insist that their first job must be called “Data
Scientist.” They may start as a Data Analyst, BI Analyst or Operations Analyst and progress from there.
Learners who struggle are often waiting to feel completely ready. But in technology, nobody ever feels
completely ready because the tools keep changing.
Strong closing line
The successful learner does not wait for confidence before taking action. Confidence usually comes after
taking action repeatedly.
Learner Story 1: The Operations Professional

before presenting it as a real encounter.
One learner who stayed with me was “Daniel,” a mid-career professional in his early forties.

• What data do we need?
• How do we clean it?
• What does the result tell us?
• How do we explain it to someone else?
When learners see that process repeatedly, their confidence grows.
Personal observation
I have seen learners without a technical background perform better than technically stronger learners
because they were curious, consistent and willing to ask questions.
Strong closing line
You do not need to be good at everything before starting. You need the willingness to practise, make
mistakes and improve.
Q3. Data science courses can be theoretical and dry. Are we doing
anything different at Lithan?
Main answer
Yes. What makes the learning different is that we do not want learners to study tools only for the sake of
passing an assessment.
At Lithan, the emphasis is on applied and work-integrated learning. Learners work on projects where they
need to take a business problem, examine the data, perform the analysis and present a recommendation.
Lithan describes its approach as a 70:20:10 work-integrated learning model, supported by industry
mentoring and real-world projects. The Data Science pathway also includes project evaluation based on
areas such as the quality of the analysis, the tools used and the practicality of the proposed solution.
Instead of simply saying, “Here is a machine-learning algorithm,” we try to ask:
• Why are we using this algorithm?
• What business problem does it solve?
• Is the data reliable?
• How will we measure whether the solution works?
• Can a non-technical stakeholder understand the result?
Learners may work on dashboards, predictive models, customer analysis, operational problems or other
industry-related case studies. They also have to explain and defend their decisions.
That presentation component is important because, in the workplace, it is not enough to produce a model.
You must convince someone to trust and use your findings.

PDDS Podcast Speaking Guide
Opening
Thank you for having me. I work closely with adult learners and career changers, so what I hope to share
today is not only what the data industry looks like, but also what I have observed from people who are
trying to enter it.
Q1. Is data science still a hot career today?
Main answer
Yes, data science is still a strong career area, but the market has evolved.
A few years ago, many companies wanted one general “data scientist” who could handle everything—from
dashboards and reporting to machine learning. Today, the work has become more specialised.
Companies are still investing in data, AI and automation, but the opportunities may appear under different
job titles.
For career changers, some of the more realistic entry points are:
• Data Analyst
• Business Analyst
• Business Intelligence Analyst
• Reporting or Operations Analyst
• Marketing, Risk or Financial Analyst
• Junior Data Engineer
• Analytics Engineer
More advanced roles include Data Scientist, Machine Learning Engineer and AI Engineer. These usually
require stronger programming, mathematics or software-engineering experience.
Singapore’s Career Conversion Programme continues to identify Data Analyst and Associate Data Engineer
as roles with longer-term prospects. The role descriptions emphasise practical abilities such as cleaning
data, producing dashboards, supporting business decisions and communicating insights—not only building
complex AI models.
Pay and prospects
Pay depends greatly on the company, industry, experience and technical level.
1

He had spent more than ten years working in logistics and operations. He understood delivery schedules,
manpower planning and operational delays, but he had almost no coding experience.
During the first few Python sessions, he was visibly frustrated. Every error message made him feel that he
did not belong in the programme.
At one point, he told me, “I think I am too old for this. Everyone else understands the code faster than me.”
Instead of focusing on Python immediately, I asked him to describe a problem from his previous workplace.
He explained that the company regularly experienced delivery delays but relied mainly on manual reports
and the supervisors’ personal judgement.
That became his project.
He analysed delivery records, identified patterns behind late deliveries and created a dashboard showing
which locations, time periods and operational conditions were associated with delays.
His coding was not the most advanced in the class. However, his project was strong because he understood
the business problem deeply.
The most memorable moment was during his presentation. He was no longer talking like a nervous
student. He was speaking like an operations professional using data to support a decision.
The lesson for me was that career changers are not starting from zero. Their domain knowledge can
become their advantage.
Short takeaway
We did not replace his logistics experience. We helped him strengthen it with data skills.

For one project, she wanted to build the most accurate model possible. She kept changing algorithms and
adjusting parameters, but she could not clearly explain what business decision the model was supposed to
support.
I asked her a simple question: “Who will use your model on Monday morning, and what will they do
differently because of it?”
She could not answer.
We went back and simplified the project. She focused on identifying customers who were likely to stop
purchasing and created a clear recommendation for how the business could prioritise its retention efforts.
Her final model was technically simpler than her original version, but the project became much stronger
because the outcome was understandable and actionable.
The unforgettable moment was when she said, “I thought data science was about showing how advanced
my model is. Now I realise it is about helping someone make a better decision.”
Short takeaway
A successful data professional does not use the most complicated tool. They use the right tool for the
problem.

Do not be discouraged by the number of tools you see online.
You do not need to master Python, SQL, Power BI, cloud computing, statistics and machine learning all at
once.
Start with one business problem. Learn how to collect the data, clean it, analyse it and explain what you
found.

healthcare, retail, logistics, education or another industry, that knowledge can help you ask better
questions than someone who only understands the technology.

A career changer entering through an analyst role should be realistic: the first job may not immediately
come with a “data scientist” title or a very high salary. One Lithan-linked career conversion programme
previously indicated an illustrative starting salary of around S$4,000 a month for a Data Analyst, while
noting that actual salary depends on qualifications, skills and experience. Current job advertisements can
vary widely; for example, a recent junior data-scientist posting advertised S$3,000 to S$8,000 monthly.
These examples should be treated as broad references, not guaranteed market rates.
The long-term prospects are strong for people who can combine three things:
1. Technical skills
2. Business or industry knowledge
3. The ability to explain insights and create business value
My advice is not to focus too much on the title. Your first position could be Data Analyst, Operations Analyst
or BI Analyst. Once you gain real experience, you can move into more specialised and better-paying roles.
Strong closing line
So, data science is not disappearing. It is becoming broader, more specialised and more connected to AI,
engineering and business decision-making.
Q2. Is data science only for people who are already strong in maths
or coding?
Main answer
That is one of the biggest misconceptions.
You do need some mathematics and coding, but you do not need to be an expert before you begin. You
develop these skills gradually through practice.
For most entry-level analytics work, learners first need to understand practical concepts such as
percentages, averages, trends, relationships between variables and basic statistics. They do not necessarily
need advanced mathematics on day one.
The same applies to coding. At the beginning, the objective is not to become a software engineer. The
objective is to use tools such as Excel, SQL, Power BI or Python to solve a problem.
From my experience, learners usually struggle not because they lack intelligence, but because they become
intimidated. They see a long piece of code or a mathematical formula and immediately conclude, “This is
not for me.”
As facilitators, our role is to break the problem into smaller steps:
• What business question are we answering?

need to take a business problem, examine the data, perform the analysis and present a recommendation.
Lithan describes its approach as a 70:20:10 work-integrated learning model, supported by industry
mentoring and real-world projects. The Data Science pathway also includes project evaluation based on
areas such as the quality of the analysis, the tools used and the practicality of the proposed solution.
Instead of simply saying, “Here is a machine-learning algorithm,” we try to ask:
• Why are we using this algorithm?
• What business problem does it solve?
• Is the data reliable?
• How will we measure whether the solution works?
• Can a non-technical stakeholder understand the result?
Learners may work on dashboards, predictive models, customer analysis, operational problems or other
industry-related case studies. They also have to explain and defend their decisions.
That presentation component is important because, in the workplace, it is not enough to produce a model.
You must convince someone to trust and use your findings.
